newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Neutral Swiss to join NATO partnership plan.
newsitem.headline: Neutral Swiss to join NATO partnership plan.

text.p: Neutral Switzerland edged away from its traditonal isolationism on Wednesday by announcing it would join NATO's Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme in a bid to promote security in post-Cold War Europe.

But the government took pains to ensure the conservative majority of Swiss that the move did not jeopardise the country's treasured neutrality nor signal its intention to join the Western military alliance.

"The federal council (cabinet) wants to make clear that participating in PFP does not create any obligations under international law and does not affect neutrality," a statement issued after the cabinet met in Berne said.
"The federal council will make clear that Switzerland is neutral and does not want to enter NATO."
The cabinet authorised Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti to sign the necessary documents.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana later told a news conference in Stockholm he expected Switzerland to officially join PFP on December 11.

The 16-member North Atlantic Treaty Organisation launched the PFP scheme in 1994, primarily to help foster ties with its former Warsaw Pact adversaries who embraced democracy after the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe.

NATO used the scheme to bolster links with emerging democracies eager to shelter under the alliance's security shield, and was seen by many of them as a half-way house to membership of the alliance. But NATO stopped short of offering its partners security guarantees that could anger a suspicious Russia.

The scheme now includes 27 partner countries, including other neutrals Finland, Austria and Sweden. All the countries in central and eastern Europe belong, as well as all the former Soviet republics except Tajikistan.
Conservative parties in Switzerland have suggested that signing up to PFP is the first step toward Swiss membership in NATO, which has emerged from the Cold War as the bedrock of Europe's security.
They have criticised the government's decision to press ahead with the plan without calling a referendum on it.
But the government, eager to boost its international role, has lobbied hard for the programme.
"Switzerland does not want to stay on the sidelines," Defence Minister Adolf Ogi told reporters earlier this month.

"We do not want to become a member of NATO but we want to take part in Partnership for Peace because we think it is important that we show Europe and the world that we can contribute something as a country of four different cultures, four different languages and 26 states," Ogi said.

"We have direct democracy, a federal system, and we have proved since 1848 that we can live together in peace and freedom. Therefore I think we are the most international country and Europe and I think we can give other countries something."

Swiss officers will observe -- but not join -- military manoeuvres and take part in peacekeeping exercises. The government remains blocked by a 1993 referendum from ever sending armed peacekeepers abroad.
